Uprising
UP-ry-zing
n. (the act of rising up; getting up from rest)
Hebrew qum, to rise or stand up. The Authorized Version pairs it with downsitting to render a Hebrew idiom for the whole of ordinary life — sitting down and getting up, the two commonest acts a body performs.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off. The pairing is an idiom, and it is chosen for its ordinariness. Downsitting and uprising are not significant events; they are what a man does dozens of times a day without noticing. David is saying that God's knowledge of him extends to the parts of his life that are too trivial to record. The psalm then moves inward in the same breath — thou understandest my thought afar off — and outward in the verses following: thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways. The doctrine is omniscience, and David develops it in the most personal terms available: God's knowledge of him is exhaustive, immediate, and comfortable rather than threatening. That last point is where the psalm differs sharply from the modern instinct. Being fully known is now widely experienced as exposure; David treats it as the ground of security, which is why the psalm that begins with total knowledge ends with an invitation to more of it — Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts. A man who has something to hide does not pray that. The middle of the psalm draws the further conclusion that there is nowhere outside this knowledge: whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), under UPRISING: the act of rising; act of rising up; ascent.

UPRISING, n. The act of rising; act of rising up.

UPRISE, v.i. To rise from a bed or seat; to get up.

DOWNSITTING, n. The act of sitting down; repose; a resting.

OMNISCIENCE, n. The knowledge of all things; infinite or unbounded knowledge; an attribute of God only.

Key Scripture

Psalm 139:2 — "Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off."

Psalm 139:1 — "O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me."

Psalm 139:3 — "Thou compassest my path and my lying down, and art acquainted with all my ways."

Psalm 139:7 — "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?"

Modern Corruption

Divine omniscience is denied outright by open theism and felt as surveillance by a culture that prizes privacy; David treats exhaustive knowledge as the ground of comfort and asks for more of it.

expand to see more

Open theism, following Pinnock, Boyd, and Sanders, holds that God does not exhaustively know the future free acts of his creatures, and adjusts the doctrine of omniscience accordingly. Psalm 139 makes that adjustment difficult. God knows the psalmist's thought afar off, is acquainted with all his ways, and — in the verses that follow — saw his substance yet being unperfect, and in God's book all his members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them. That is knowledge of a life before it was lived. The classical doctrine is not a philosophical imposition on the text; the text is where the doctrine comes from.

The cultural resistance is different and more widely felt. In an age formed by surveillance, to be fully known sounds like exposure, and the psalm is read with a shiver. David's response runs the other way, and it ends in a request: Search me, O God, and know my heart. The difference is not temperament but standing. A man under judgment fears to be known; a man in covenant with God finds that being known is the only ground on which he can be loved as he actually is, rather than as he has presented himself. The doctrine cuts both ways, as the psalm itself acknowledges in its severe middle section, and the believer's comfort is that the One who misses nothing has set his love on him anyway.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qum (H6965), to rise up; shebeth (H3427), sitting down; yada (H3045), to know; chaqar (H2713), to search out.

expand to see more

Hebrew qum (H6965) — to arise, to stand up; rendered uprising.

Hebrew shebeth (H3427) — to sit, to dwell; rendered downsitting, the other half of the idiom.

Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; the psalm's governing verb.

Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out, to examine thoroughly; the psalm's first and last request.

Hebrew rea (H7454) — thought, purpose; understood afar off.

Usage

"“my downsitting and mine uprising” — an idiom for the whole of ordinary life."

"“thou understandest my thought afar off” — the knowledge reaching inward."

"“whither shall I flee from thy presence?” — nowhere outside it."
